title: Sacrifice as knowledge (4.24–4.33)
hook: the verse many families say before dinner, and a list of a dozen ways to make an offering

segments.voice: Yesterday: akarma, action without attachment. Your line was free while acting. Did you catch your grip on a result, and loosen a finger? Day one hundred seventy-three.

In some Hindu homes, and in some school dining halls in India, the food is served, everyone waits, and a short Sanskrit verse is chanted before anyone eats. Some children learn it by ear long before they know what it means. Brahmarpanam, it begins. It's a grace before meals, and it comes from today's reading, Gita chapter four, verse twenty-four. What's surprising is what it says. It doesn't thank anyone for the food. It says the food, the eater, the fire and the offering are all one thing. Today: why a verse about fire ended up at the dinner table.
screen: `THE FOOD IS SERVED. EVERYONE WAITS.` → `BRAHMARPANAM.` → `A VERSE AT THE DINNER TABLE.`

segments.voice: In the old Vedic sacrifice, the yajna, a priest pours ghee into a fire, and the fire carries the offering to the gods. Verse twenty-four takes that whole scene and turns it inside out. The act of offering is Brahman, it says. The offering is Brahman. It's poured by Brahman into the fire, which is Brahman. And the one who sees Brahman in the action reaches Brahman. Every part of the ritual is the same reality. So when families chant it over a plate of rice, the meal becomes the fire, the eating becomes the offering. Then Krishna lists the ways people sacrifice, and the list keeps widening. Some offer to the gods. Some offer their senses into the fire of self-control. Some offer their wealth. Some offer austerity, or yoga, or the study of scripture. Some offer the in-breath into the out-breath, and the out-breath into the in-breath. Even breathing can be a sacrifice. And then verse thirty-three ranks them. Better than any offering of things, Krishna says, is the offering of knowledge, because all action ends in knowledge. The fire has moved inside. What gets burned now isn't ghee. It's ignorance. A few verses later he says it outright: as a blazing fire turns wood to ash, the fire of knowledge turns karma to ash. That's the word today, sacrifice as knowledge. Seeing clearly is itself the offering, and the seeing burns.
screen: `THE FIRE, THE GHEE, THE PRIEST.` · `ALL OF IT IS BRAHMAN.` · `EVEN BREATH CAN BE AN OFFERING.` · `THE OFFERING OF KNOWLEDGE.` · then, large: `KNOWLEDGE BURNS KARMA.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-nine makes breathing an offering, so let's try it. Sit comfortably. Breathe in slowly, and as you do, think: this is given. Breathe out, and think: this is given back. Nothing to fix, nothing to earn. Just the in-breath and the out-breath, each one handed to the other. If your mind wanders, that's fine; bring it back to the next breath. If you pray, you can offer the breath to God. The bell holds the time.
Yajna. Sacrifice, offering: the old fire ritual moved inward. Seeing clearly is the highest offering, and the fire it lights burns karma.
Your line: knowledge burns karma. Before one meal today, pause for a single breath and look at the plate as if it were an offering. Day one hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Some Hindu families, schools and ashrams chant Gita 4.24 (brahmarpanam) as a grace before meals; the idea of offering breath, study and work as yajna shapes daily practice for some.

match.prompt: what's inside the fire — tap the pairs.

myth: in the Gita, sacrifice only means rituals with fire
Krishna's list includes self-control, wealth, study, yoga and even the breath.
the brahmarpanam verse is used as a grace before meals
some families and schools chant Gita 4.24 before eating.
Krishna says an offering of things beats an offering of knowledge
verse 33 says the reverse: knowledge is higher, since all action ends in it.

fork.setup: Krishna lists many kinds of offering: to the gods, of wealth, of study, of the breath. which does he call the highest?
fork.reveal: knowledge. verse 33: all action culminates in knowledge, so the offering of knowledge is higher than any offering of things.

original.note: Sanskrit: yajna, sacrifice or offering; the fire ritual of the Vedas, which the Gita widens to all of life.

trapdoor: what you thought: sacrifice means giving something up.
what it means: every act can be an offering, and seeing clearly is the highest one; its fire burns karma.
what a scholar hears: verse 24 maps each part of the Vedic yajna (the ladle, the ghee, the fire, the priest) onto Brahman; the fire image returns in 4.37, where knowledge burns all karma to ash.
